pass_a_gloss: Cyril: Altogether so. For the matter is full of godlessness. And one would reasonably also range with these and number together the thinking that human things are administered by others’ nods, and that the authority of the things according to us has been hung not upon ourselves, but upon those whom the inventors of such unpersuasive doctrines should choose to myth-mold. For Heimarmenē / Fate and Tychē / Fortune and Genesis / birth-lot, I do not know how, setting them as it were some steersmen over the life, they say each of us is not a willer or lord of the things to be done; yet to be led as from a necessary bond toward what seems to those ruling. Then what would ever become more irrational than such a thing? And how would Satan have done greater injustice to the race of humans, than when he disposed them to think and reason thus? For how would someone still counsel the useful things, and go willingly-working upon them ever? And having come to be also in the more shameful things, and having thought what one must not, how would he accuse himself and having melted with griefs change counsel to think and do the better things? For just as for those darting through the sea and having chosen to sail through there is somehow every necessity to be led by winds from the stern, and to be forced everywhere toward what seems to the pushing-together; so somewhere altogether also for us ourselves it is necessary to yield, unto whatever Fortune should choose to ferry, and the hard-to-flee winds of Fate according to them. Or will you yourself also think again that these things have been said rightly? Palladius: For how not? Cyril: Therefore it is altogether silly to crown the good and fair one with praises, and to count him worthy of honor, yet to count the wicked and unbridled one abominable and spat-upon. Palladius: In what manner do you say? Cyril: Because, O Palladius, Genesis / birth-lot and Tychē / Fortune have conquered according to them, and unwillingly they carry off upon both the thrice-wretched race of those upon the earth. And nothing voluntary is beside us. Or is not what has been born to move something and is able, a cause of being moved for those moved from it? Palladius: I say so. Cyril: Come then through equal thoughts unto the human things, and measure the things according to us, and in order that you may look around well at what evil we are in, if not by our own voluntary leanings we go either this way or that way and hurry through, yet we have been overpowered as it were and have been carried under by others’ yokes able to lead and carry the things according to us, whichever way they should choose. For already thinking the likely things, we will still ascribe nothing of the things to be done to ourselves, yet rather we will hang the causes upon all upon those accustomed to helm unto whatever according to their judgment. Therefore just as the just one will stand off from every praise, so also the unjust from penalty, and from needing to be punished. Palladius: You reason most rightly. Cyril: In vain therefore the inventors of such doctrines admire Solon the one at Athens,
